Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: No credible primary-source evidence found in this research run for a Benin-specific consumer protection framework for digital payments (e.g., payment dispute resolution rules, e-money user rights) published by regulator or in statute. BCEAO-related commentary notes consumer protection is within the applicable legal/regulatory provisions for payment institutions, but this is not Benin-specific and no underlying consumer protection legal text was captured ([Cabinet Houda summary of UEMOA Instruction n°001-01-2024](https://www.avocatshouda.com/en/uemoa-instruction-n001-01-2024-on-payment-services-in-umoa-member-states-comesinto-force/)).

revision_notes: Original score was 0/Unknown with no source cited. A light check surfaced BCEAO/UEMOA Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services (binding on Benin as a UMOA member state, containing governance, internal-control and data-consent obligations for payment institutions), the OQSF-Benin national financial complaints platform due to launch Q1 2026, and a World Bank Benin Financial Sector Review recommending strengthened consumer protection — together indicating general, non-payment-specific protection exists rather than a dedicated framework. Moved from fast path (Unknown/no source) to full path and rescored 0 -> 2 (Partial) based on these fetched sources.
revised_comments: Benin's payment services are subject to BCEAO/UEMOA Instruction No. 001-01-2024 on payment services, which imposes governance, internal control and data-consent safeguards on payment institutions, but does not set out a dedicated payment-specific consumer protection regime covering disclosure, liability allocation or error resolution. General consumer protection therefore rests on the broader banking and microfinance regulatory framework. A national financial-sector complaints platform, to be run by the Observatory for the Quality of Financial Services of Benin (OQSF-Benin) with Luxembourg cooperation funding, is scheduled to launch in the first quarter of 2026, indicating that consumer-protection mechanisms for digital financial services are still being built out rather than comprehensive.

Definition: Whether legal or regulatory requirements obligate payment service providers to notify users, regulators, and/or data protection authorities about payment data breaches, cybersecurity incidents, or unauthorized access within specified timeframes.
Comments: No credible primary-source evidence found in this research run for a Benin law/regulation that imposes explicit data breach notification requirements (mandatory or discretionary) applicable to payment service providers. Searches included “Benin data breach notification”, “notification violation données Bénin”, and cybersecurity incident reporting related to payments; no authoritative legal text was identified.

revision_notes: Original score was 0/Unknown with no source cited. A light check surfaced Article 427 of Benin's Digital Code (Law 2017-20 of 20 April 2018, amended by Law 2020-35 of 6 January 2021), a mandatory breach-notification provision applicable to all personal-data controllers including payment service providers, confirmed via DLA Piper's Data Protection Laws of the World guide and the primary legal text reproduced on ICT Policy Africa. Moved from fast path to full path and rescored 0 -> 3 (Mandatory).
revised_comments: Benin's Digital Code (Law No. 2017-20 of 20 April 2018, as amended by Law No. 2020-35 of 6 January 2021) imposes a mandatory data-breach notification requirement on all data controllers, including payment service providers. Article 427 requires the controller to notify the data protection authority (Autorité de Protection des Données à caractère Personnel, APDP) and the affected data subject without delay, describing the nature and likely consequences of the breach and the remedial steps taken. Secondary commentary describes a working expectation of notification within 72 hours where feasible.

Comments: No credible primary-source evidence found in this research run for a Benin data protection law (or WAEMU-level equivalent) that clearly covers personal data and applies to payment data. Searches included “Benin data privacy law”, “protection des données Bénin”, and BCEAO/WAEMU personal data protection references; results returned only secondary mentions without the underlying statute text.

revision_notes: Original score was 0/Unknown with no source cited. A light check surfaced Benin's Digital Code (Law 2017-20, amended 2020-35) and Law 2009-09 on protection of personal data, both confirmed via DLA Piper's Data Protection Laws of the World guide and official Beninese legal texts (SGG, APDP archive). These constitute general data protection legislation applicable to personal data, including payment data, but no payment-specific provisions were identified. Moved from fast path to full path and rescored 0 -> 2 (General Data Protection Legislation).
revised_comments: Benin has general data protection legislation covering personal data, including payment transaction data, under the Digital Code (Law No. 2017-20 of 20 April 2018, amended by Law No. 2020-35 of 6 January 2021, Book V) and the earlier Law No. 2009-09 of 22 May 2009 on the protection of personally identifiable information. These establish data subject rights (access, rectification, objection, portability, erasure) and an independent regulator, the Autorité de Protection des Données à caractère Personnel (APDP). The legislation is general in scope and contains no payment-specific data provisions.

A light check surfaced a Benin government (gouv.bj) report on an August 2024 workshop on disability inclusion in decentralised financial services, referencing Law 2017-06 on disability rights. This source concerns the broader financial-services/SFD sector rather than digital-payment access points specifically, and describes a stocktaking/reflection process rather than completed implementation. Moved to full path and tentatively rescored 0 -> 1 (No/limited accommodation), but flagged for human review given the indirect fit to the variable's specific scope (payment apps/USSD/agent accessibility) and the absence of Benin-specific evidence on accessible payment design.
revised_comments: Benin adopted Law No. 2017-06 of 29 September 2017 on the protection and promotion of the rights of persons with disabilities, which obliges private-sector service providers, including decentralised financial system (SFD) operators, to take measures accommodating persons with disabilities. A government-convened workshop in Cotonou in August 2024, held by the Ministry of Social Affairs and Microfinance together with the professional association of decentralised financial systems (APSFD), was framed as an initial stocktaking exercise to identify approaches to end the exclusion of persons with disabilities still observed in parts of the sector, indicating that accessible design features in payment access points remain limited rather than systematically implemented.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: No credible Benin-specific evidence found in this research run of policies/programs explicitly enabling refugees/migrants to access digital payments (e.g., refugee-acceptable KYC for mobile money, UNHCR cash program in Benin using mobile money). Searches for Benin refugee financial inclusion and KYC evidence did not yield authoritative Benin sources.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original score was 0/Unknown with no source cited. A light check surfaced the WFP Benin Country Brief (August 2023), confirming beneficiaries without ID cards cannot open mobile money accounts, and the Benin Gulf of Guinea Joint Response Plan Report (UNHCR-coordinated, 2024), describing accelerating refugee/IDP registration and a planned 2025 WURI-supported enrolment of refugees in the National Register of Natural Persons (RNPP) to provide identification facilitating access to national services. Moved from fast path to full path and rescored 0 -> 2 (Partial): documentation pathways are emerging for registered refugees/IDPs, but undocumented displaced people remain excluded from standard account opening.
revised_comments: Refugees, asylum-seekers and internally displaced persons in northern Benin face practical barriers accessing digital payment accounts: mobile money accounts require an identity document, and undocumented displaced people cannot open one, requiring WFP and partners to distribute access codes to beneficiaries lacking ID cards so they can receive cash-based assistance (WFP Benin, 2023). Registration of refugees and IDPs has since accelerated, with over 20,000 refugees and asylum-seekers and around 12,500 IDPs registered by end-2024 through the national asylum authority (SP-CNRA) and the civil protection agency (ABPC), and the World Bank-supported WURI project plans to enrol refugees in the National Register of Natural Persons (RNPP) from 2025, issuing a unique identification number intended to facilitate access to national services including financial services. Access therefore depends on registration status: documented refugees and IDPs have an emerging pathway to formal identification and inclusion in national registries, while undocumented individuals remain excluded from standard mobile money account opening and rely on humanitarian workarounds.
